summary: How the United States came to jail children at record rates from the 1970s on: courts eroding juvenile rights, the superpredator panic, zero-tolerance policing in schools, and abusive for-profit youth prisons run by James Slattery.

evidence.note: story opens with the 1964 Gault case and the 1967 Supreme Court ruling
courts reverse course in the late 1970s, culminating in Schall v. Martin in 1984
New York's 1978 law lets 13-year-olds be tried as adults; other states follow
DiIulio and Wilson's superpredator prediction drives harsher laws in the 1990s
after Columbine, armed officers and zero-tolerance discipline spread through schools
high-stakes testing in Florida and Texas pushes suspensions; Texas Miracle and NCLB
Black, Latino and disabled students disproportionately referred to police and arrested
2015 Lynchburg case of an 11-year-old autistic boy charged with felony assault
long segment on Slattery, from slum hotels to for-profit youth prisons
abuse, maggot-filled food and beatings at the Pahokee youth facility in Florida
teen dies of untreated pneumonia at a company boot camp near Fort Worth in 2001
closing notes cities pulling police out of schools as of 2020

notes: No subject kind fits a systemic policy trend well; school-to-prison pipeline entered as practice-or-pseudoscience. Slattery's birth and death years are not given, so floruit 1996 (move to Florida and youth prisons) is used. Florida and Texas both get long segments, so no single subdivision. main_span ends at the 2015 school-cop cases; the trend continues at release.
